catalog_quote: As common in Bantu, Cuwabo has a binary tone system, intertwining high (H) and toneless (Ø) pitches. In this study, H tones are indicated by means of an acute accent. [...] The tone-bearing unit in Cuwabo is the mora, which represents the smallest phonological unit in a syllabic nucleus (Hayes 1989, Hyman 1992). [...] The great majority of Cuwabo words have at least one primary H tone [...]. In fact, only a few grammatical words (e.g. akala 'if') and ideophones can have an all-low tone pattern. [...] This falling H, manifested phonetically by a pitch lowering, results from the position of the mora receiving the doubled H, namely the penultimate of a prosodic unit [...]. new_statements.quote: As common in Bantu, Cuwabo has a binary tone system, intertwining high (H) and toneless (Ø) pitches. [...] The tone-bearing unit in Cuwabo is the mora, which represents the smallest phonological unit in a syllabic nucleus [...] (p. 86) [...] Finally, unlike many eastern Bantu languages such as Chewa, Swahili, Mwani (Devos 2008), Makonde (Manus 2003, Kraal 2005), Cuwabo is not subject to penultimate lengthening at the end of a prosodic unit (although the falling H may be viewed as reminiscent of a system formerly marked by penultimate lengthening, as already stated above). (p. 88)

new_statements.rule_in_words: Cuwabo is described purely as a tone language (privative H vs Ø, mora as TBU, lexical and grammatical tone, tonal minimal pairs); the grammar makes no statement about word stress or accent and explicitly denies the phrase-penultimate lengthening typical of eastern Bantu. The only positional regularities are tonal: every word surfaces with at least one H, underlyingly toneless nouns receive a predictable H on the second mora of the word (first stem mora after a prefix), and a doubled H landing on the penult of a prosodic unit is realised as a falling tone.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed (no stress analysis at all).
new_statements.exceptions: A few grammatical words (e.g. akala 'if') and ideophones may be all-low. The author notes (p. 22) that the 1989 orthography standardisation report claimed general penultimate vowel lengthening ('todas as vogais sofrem um alongamento, geralmente na penúltima sílaba') and rejects this as not attested synchronically; the penult falling contour (p. 86) is offered as a possible relic of former penultimate lengthening.
new_statements.domain_note: Tone patterns given for citation forms (nouns uttered sentence-finally); the falling realisation of a doubled H and the (absent) lengthening are stated for the right edge of a prosodic unit/phrase, not the word. Section 3.6.3 treats extra-high pitch on certain moras as intonational 'rhetorical emphasis', not lexical stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Guérois 2015 is explicitly based on central Cuwabo, the variety spoken around Quelimane and Macuse (Zambezia), as opposed to the Karungu, Mayindo, Marale/Manyawa and Nyaringa dialects (thesis p. ~10-11). Same language as Glottolog chuw1238 / ISO chw (spelled Chuwabu, Chuwabo, Cuwabo, Ecuwabo, Echuwabo, Txuwabo, Xuabo).

sources.note: Ch. 3 'Tones' (pp. 85-142): binary H vs toneless system, TBU = mora, lexical and grammatical tone with minimal pairs; every word surfaces with at least one H; toneless nouns get a predictable H on the 2nd mora of the word (pp. 98-99). The word 'stress' never occurs in the phonology; explicitly states Cuwabo has NO penultimate lengthening (pp. 50, 88, 521, conclusion ~p. 565), though a doubled H on the penult of a prosodic unit surfaces as a falling tone, 'reminiscent' of former penult lengthening (p. 86).
